name: Fatima Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary day of music work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, teach four beginner singers, record backing vocals when the studio calls and sing a paid Sunday set with our local choir. I left school after secondary classes and still learn by watching the more experienced singers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is satisfying, and what wears on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a child hearing her own clear note. My partner repairs buses, and our two children and mortgage mean a late studio call can scramble who collects them after school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AI Plateau may shorten booking messages, but somebody still has to hear whether a child is singing too high. My four beginner pupils and the Sunday paid set would stay as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner repairs buses and earns steady wages, and we have about three months of bills saved. I watch our mortgage, but one delayed studio call would not put us behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the four lessons and the confirmed Sunday set this month. I’d ask the studio to put the next backing-vocal fee in writing before I arrange a school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work in this picture. Late studio calls still irritate me, but the household could cover one missed afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one cancelled studio date mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One backing-vocal date pays for a week of food, so I would check whether the studio owes a cancellation fee. I would not count it until the agreement is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI lesson sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and do not want to try one on a pupil’s voice. A child needs me to stop the song and listen, not hand out a polished sheet.

I would accept shorter **booking messages** while keeping fees in writing.

I will not test **AI** on a pupil’s voice when I have never used it myself.
do: Keep four **voice pupils** and the confirmed Sunday set this month.
Get the next **studio fee** in writing before changing the school pickup plan.
feel: I feel **calm** about one missed afternoon while household earnings hold.
fieldNote: Her **three-month reserve** and partner’s steady repair work buffer a small recording loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the studio Steady Disruption could cut the plain backing vocals and lesson plans before it touches our live set. I would ask which sessions still pay a singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those plain parts are exactly the work a junior singer like me gets. If the studio keeps only the strongest voices, a real part of my pay disappears even while my partner keeps working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this week for its next six paid dates. If it cancels two dates in the first year, I’d ask the choir leader for an extra paid beginner rehearsal only if there is a room, families pay and my partner can collect the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own fee list getting shorter. Three months of savings buys time to ask, but not a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an extra rehearsal worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free choir space is not a paid hour for the person leading it. Five paying families would cover my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop the current lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the four current pupils until a replacement session is genuinely booked. Promising the children a new rehearsal before anyone pays would only confuse them.

I would keep the **live set** on the calendar while clients still book it.

Three months of **savings** cannot replace a permanent cut in my pay.
do: Ask the **studio** this week for its next six paid dates.

feel: I feel **anxious** about a shorter fee list despite the household reserve.
fieldNote: Her junior **backing-vocal work** faces thinking AI before live singing does.
An added **rehearsal** depends on a room, five paid families, her pay and partner pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2028 could make backing vocals, lesson plans and booking cheap very quickly. Robots able to sing hands-on work as well as people would follow around 2031, so live dates are on a later clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the studio to stop calling for plain vocals in 2028, and some parents may try AI lessons. My partner’s bus wages and three months saved would carry us briefly, but we could not replace my whole pay for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get the studio’s paid schedule now and ask the choir leader for written Sunday dates. If recording calls stop in the first year after 2028, I’d give notice on my rented practice room at renewal and seek a posted paid choir-assistant opening only if its hours and rate cover the lost fees and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed because I expect a large part of my work to go before I can build another roster. My partner's bus-repair wage cannot replace my singing income once our three-month reserve runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When could you leave the practice room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice room has a monthly fee and a notice date in the lease. I would wait for that date rather than pay a penalty to leave early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A choir-assistant post would need to be advertised and paid, not offered as good exposure. I would keep my four pupils until a written offer arrived.

fieldNote: She separates **2028 recorded work** from capable robots for live singing around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2031 gives us five years to prepare for cheaper recordings and plans. Capable robots for hands-on singing would come around 2034, so I would still check each live booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could improve my teaching with an experienced choir leader, but I am no trained vocal coach. The mortgage and children mean I cannot take unpaid evening classes just to collect a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the choir leader next term to observe one beginner lesson and ask the hall about a funded short course held outside my paid hours. If the course teaches skills parents actually need, I’d take it only when my partner can cover pickup. Next term I’d ask for a second group only if the hall gives a room and five families pay for my time. In the first year after 2031, I’d keep that group only while those fees still cover both costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing recordings, but five years gives me time to learn without dropping the pupils I already have. I would rather see one class work than buy a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the observation teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior teacher could show me where I rush a child who cannot hear the pitch yet. One observed lesson would tell me more than a certificate I cannot use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How firm is the five-family condition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the second group only if the hall confirms a room and five families actually pay. Four interested families are not the same as five paid places.

I would check every **live booking** while the recorded work changes.

fieldNote: Her **resistant** style favors observed practice and a proven course over new technology.

S3.quote: Four interested families are not the same as five paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make careful choices, with capable robots for hands-on singing around 2039. I would still ask what this Sunday’s live booking pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More pupils at 53 are a possibility, not money in our account today. My partner’s steady repair work and our three-month reserve make the next few years manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep four pupils and the paid Sunday set this year, then test an added group in coming years only if five families pay. I’d put ten from each paid studio date into separate savings after mortgage and food are covered. In the first year after 2036, I’d keep that group only while fees cover the room and my hours, and apply for a posted paid choir role only if those teaching hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about what work looks like at 53, but I am not worried about next month’s roof. A decade gives me time to test what families still pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the ten replacing existing savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten is new savings, above our current three-month reserve. I would transfer it only after the studio fee has reached the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not promise the children that music will pay their bills. I would let them learn it and also show them how a written contract protects a family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the plain backing vocals to vanish before I have more pupils. Written choir dates, a paid assistant opening and an affordable room would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether I would still sing without the studio. I would. Singing for love does not pay the mortgage, so I keep the paid dates and family bills on separate pages.

headlineQuote: Singing for love does not pay the mortgage, so I keep the paid dates and family bills on separate pages.
portrait: At **43**, Fatima teaches beginner voice, records simple backing parts and sings Sunday sets after secondary school.
Her typical **pay**, partner’s bus-repair wage and three-month reserve cushion a single cancelled session.
She avoids **AI tools** and prefers an observed lesson, a written fee and familiar choir work.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens junior recordings first; she seeks paid openings and protects childcare and mortgage money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end plain backing-vocal work before her pupil list grows.
whatWouldHelp: Written **choir dates**, a posted paid assistant opening and affordable lesson space would help.
